migrationNotes: Spine: a librarian must list every pupil even when a pupil has borrowed nothing, and the same kept-row rule is followed through what the blank means, how to count it, where a test goes and how to find the rows that matched nothing.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-preserve-the-left-table-8 (what the orders columns hold) and -9 (which column is always filled). Both are taught on the first, third and fifth screens.

lesson.title: Keep the customers with no orders

steps.headline: Keeping the pupil with no books

lead.text: An INNER JOIN works like a librarian who writes down only the lines that have a book. A row with no partner leaves no trace in the result. When a report has to list everything on one side, that is the wrong tool.

LEFT JOIN is the right one. Take customers LEFT JOIN orders. The table written first is the left table, and every one of its rows appears in the result. A customer with matching orders gets a row for each order, as before. A customer with no matching order still gets one row, and the columns that should have come from orders are filled with NULL.

That NULL has a definite meaning. It says that no order matched, so there was nothing to copy into those columns. The next screens look at how such a blank behaves when you count it, test it and filter around it.
Write the list the way the librarian would, with a line for every pupil.

steps.headline: A blank that means no match

lead.text: Now the clubs are the left table, and the pupils are the rows that may or may not be there. Art has no pupils, so no pupil satisfies the ON condition for it. An INNER JOIN would drop Art. A LEFT JOIN keeps it and fills the pupil columns with NULL.

Look at the two blanks in the second result. Di's year is NULL because the school never recorded it, and Di is a real pupil. Art's pupil and year are both NULL because no pupil matched. The same symbol sits in both places and means different things. To tell them apart, look at a column that every real pupil has, such as the pupil's id.

afterFigure.text: The first query returns four rows and the second returns five. The extra row is the club with nobody in it. Everything the inner join returned is still there, so a LEFT JOIN never loses rows from the left table and never loses a match.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Keep every club
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil, p.year FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: Six orders match their customers, and one customer, Dee, has no order. Join the tables so that every customer stays.

reveal.text: You kept every match and added the customer with none. The unmatched row is still a row of the result.

queries.label: Only matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Keep every customer
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A kept row counts as a row. COUNT(*) counts every row of the result, so a club with no pupils still adds 1 to it. Often that is not the number you want. To count matches, count a column from the other table, because COUNT(column) skips the NULLs.

Not every column of the other table is safe for this. A real pupil can have an unknown year, so COUNT(p.year) would miss Di. The key column is different. Every real pupil has an id, so COUNT(p.id) is filled on every matched row and empty only on the kept one. It counts the matches exactly.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the clubs are grouped, and the first query counts rows while the second counts pupil ids. Art has one row but no pupils, so it shows 1 in the first query and 0 in the second. The other clubs agree in both queries because every row of theirs is a real match.

queries.label: Count the rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count the pupil ids
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, COUNT(p.id) AS pupils FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: COUNT of a column ignores NULL. After the join, a customer with no match has NULL in every order column.

reveal.text: You counted matched orders, not rows. Counting a column from the right table gives zero for a customer with none.

queries.label: Count joined rows
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Count matched orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;

lead.text: A test on the other table raises a new question, because it can go in two places. Written in ON, it becomes part of the matching rule and decides which rows pair up, and a row that finds no partner is still kept with NULLs. Written in WHERE, it runs afterwards on the finished rows and removes any row that fails.

A row kept for lack of a partner has NULL in the pupil columns, and a test such as p.year = 6 is never true of NULL. In WHERE that row fails the test and disappears, so the LEFT JOIN quietly turns back into an inner join. Put the test in ON when every row of the left table has to stay.

afterFigure.text: The picture asks for the clubs with their year 6 pupils. With the test in ON, all four clubs are still listed. Chess and Choir show a year 6 pupil, and Drama and Art show NULL because nobody in year 6 matched them. With the test in WHERE, only the two clubs that have a year 6 pupil remain.

queries.label: Test in ON
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id AND p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

queries.label: Test in WHERE
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year = 6 ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: In Dee's row every orders column is NULL. A test written after the join runs on those NULLs.

reveal.text: You decided where the paid test belongs. A test in ON limits which orders match. A test in WHERE can remove the preserved customer.

queries.label: Version one
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

queries.label: Version two
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id, o.id;

lead.text: A kept row can be picked out with IS NULL, which you met earlier for unknown values. The question is which column to test. A column that the other table can leave unknown on a real row gives a muddled answer, because the test then finds both kinds of blank.

The pupils show it. Di is a real pupil whose year was never recorded, so p.year IS NULL is true for Di and for the kept row of Art. The key column p.id is filled on every real pupil, so p.id IS NULL is true only where nothing matched. Testing the key finds exactly the clubs with no pupils.

afterFigure.text: The first query tests the key and returns Art alone. The second tests the year and returns Drama and Art, which are different kinds of row. When you want the rows with no match, test a column that a matched row always has.

queries.label: Test the key
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Test the year
queries.sql: SELECT c.name AS club, p.name AS pupil FROM clubs AS c LEFT JOIN pupils AS p ON p.club = c.id WHERE p.year IS NULL ORDER BY c.id, p.id;

lead.text: The shop's customers are the left table and the orders are the other. Pick the test that finds only the customers with no order.

lesson.orientation: Preserve unmatched customers without counting them as orders.
lesson.reviewLabel: Keep the customers with no orders
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A librarian lists each pupil beside the books they have borrowed. Ann borrowed 2, Bo borrowed 1 and Cy borrowed none. The head teacher wants a list of every pupil with the books they have out, so she can see at a glance who has been using the library.

If the librarian writes only the lines that have a book, Cy never appears, and the list suggests that the school has two pupils. To show everyone she writes a line for Cy as well and leaves the book blank. The blank has a definite meaning: no book matched Cy.

The last lesson's join drops a row that has no partner. This lesson keeps it, and shows how to count and test the blanks that result, so that a missing partner is never mistaken for a missing value inside a row that did have one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll keep customers who have no orders, and tell a missing match from a missing amount.

recap.keyIdea: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table and fills the other table's columns with NULL where nothing matched. Count and test the other table's key to tell a missing match from a missing value.

blocks.text: You wrote 4 lines for 3 pupils and counted 7 rows once Dee was kept. Her COUNT(o.id) was 0, because no order matched.

recap.nextHook: A LEFT JOIN protects only the table written first. Sometimes both lists have people missing from the other: guests who replied but have no badge, and badges printed for people who never replied. Keeping everyone from both sides is the next step.

questions.prompt: How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
hints: Keep each order match.
Add one row for the customer with no match.
Add Dee's preserved unmatched row to the six order matches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six matched order rows plus Dee's unmatched customer row make seven.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Six order matches stay, and Dee adds one preserved row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the matches alone. Dee still has to appear.

questions.prompt: For Dee after the LEFT JOIN, what does COUNT(o.id) return?
hints: COUNT(column) ignores NULL.
The retained customer row has a NULL order id.
Dee's order id is NULL; COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL matched keys.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Dee has no matched order id, so COUNT(o.id) is zero.

questions.onCorrect: 0. COUNT of a column skips NULL, and Dee's order id is NULL.

misconceptions.feedback: COUNT(*) would count her kept row. COUNT of a column skips NULL.

questions.prompt: Where should o.status = 'paid' go if every customer must remain?
hints: Preserve the customer while restricting which orders match.

acceptedIdeas: In ON as a matching condition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Put the paid condition in ON to limit which orders match while preserving every left-side customer. A WHERE test on the right-side status would remove unmatched customer rows.

choices.label: In ON as a matching condition
In WHERE as the only row filter

questions.onCorrect: In ON as a matching condition. That limits which orders match and keeps every customer.

misconceptions.feedback: Dee's order columns are NULL, so a test after the join drops her row.
An alias names a column. It cannot filter rows.

questions.prompt: Which predicate identifies customers with no matched order?
hints: An actual order can have a missing amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The joined order id is NULL when no order matched. Because stored order ids are non-NULL, o.id IS NULL identifies those unmatched rows.

questions.onCorrect: o.id IS NULL. The order key is filled on every real match, so NULL means none matched.

misconceptions.feedback: A real order can have an unknown amount, so this finds more than the unmatched.
That keeps paid orders, so it removes unmatched customers instead of finding them.

questions.prompt: How many rows remain with the paid test in ON for the original data?
hints: Count paid matches for each customer.
Retain one row for Dee even without a paid match.
Add Ada's two paid matches, Ben's paid match, Cy's paid match and Dee's preserved row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ada has two paid orders, Ben one and Cy one; Dee remains once with no match. Total: five.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Four paid matches, plus Dee kept as one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That drops Dee. A test in ON keeps every customer.

questions.prompt: How many rows pass o.amount IS NULL after the original LEFT JOIN?
hints: A missing amount is not the same as no order.
Inspect both the real missing amount and the unmatched customer.
Inspect order 106's missing amount and the NULL fields in Dee's unmatched row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Cy's order 106 and Dee's unmatched customer row both have NULL amounts.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Order 106 has an unknown amount, and Dee's unmatched row has NULL there too.

misconceptions.feedback: That finds only one of the two rows with a NULL amount.

questions.prompt: A librarian lists each pupil beside the books they have borrowed. Ann borrowed 2, Bo borrowed 1 and Cy borrowed none. How many lines does the list need if every pupil must appear?
hints: Each borrowed book needs its own line.
A pupil with no book still needs a line.
Add Ann's lines and Bo's line, then one line for Cy.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ann has two lines and Bo has one. Cy still needs a line, so there are four.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A pupil with no book still gets a line, with the book left blank. A LEFT JOIN keeps rows the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves Cy off. Every pupil has to appear, even with no book.

questions.prompt: In a LEFT JOIN, what do the orders columns hold for a customer with no matching order?
hints: Is there any order to take values from?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No order matched, so there is nothing to show. The orders columns are left empty, as NULL.

questions.onCorrect: NULL. A preserved customer gets NULL in every column of the table that did not match.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero would claim a known amount. An unmatched row has no value at all.
Nothing is copied from other rows. Unmatched columns are left empty.

questions.prompt: Which orders column is always filled on a matched order, so counting it counts the matches?
hints: Which column of an order can never be unknown?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every real order has an id, even when its amount is unknown, so o.id is filled on each match.

questions.onCorrect: o.id. A matched order always has its key, even when another column is unknown.

misconceptions.feedback: An order can be real while its amount is unknown. Pick a column that is always filled.
A status can be unknown too. Pick the column that names the order.

questions.prompt: Customers X, Y and Z have 4, 0 and 0 orders. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
hints: How many rows does X contribute?
Each customer with no order still contributes a row.
Add X's rows and one row for each of the others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: X gives four rows. Y and Z each give one preserved row, so six rows in all.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Each match is a row, and each customer with no match is kept as one row.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the two customers with no orders. A LEFT JOIN keeps each of them as a row.
